items.q: When Do I Get Paid Commission?
items.a: First fortnightly pay cycle of the month — once a month, like clockwork. The figure is built from cash that's actually arrived in MEC's bank account that month, not from bookings you've quoted or even confirmed. Customer pays → you get paid. The Payments module in Zoho is where every dollar gets tracked back to the booking and back to you.

items.q: What is the True-up?
items.a: Monthly commission is an honest estimate, not gospel. At quarter-end we run the proper quarterly bands math against what you actually delivered. If we paid you too much, the excess sits as a balance and nets against next month's commission — your bank account never goes backwards. If we paid you too little, next month tops you up. Your base salary stays untouched either way.

items.q: What if a Booking I Made Gets Cancelled or Refunded?
items.a: Refunds aren't fun, but here's how it works: the refunded amount shows as negative cash on the booking in Zoho, and gets netted against your next commission cycle. Your base salary is never touched, and your paycheck never goes negative — at worst, that month's commission gets a bit thinner. We move on.

items.q: How is my Band Rate Calculated?
items.a: Your annual GP received climbs through bands like rungs on a ladder. The first chunk earns at rate A%, the next chunk at a higher rate, the next at higher again. The further you climb, the more you earn per dollar of GP — that's the whole point of a banded structure. The 'Effective Rate' shown on your dashboard is your blended average across every band you've already climbed through.

items.q: Why Monthly Bands Instead of Quarterly or Annual?
items.a: Cash flow. Annual bands would mean waiting until December to see a single dollar of commission — no thanks. Monthly bands keep money landing in your account regularly. The quarterly true-up keeps it fair: monthly is the estimate, quarterly is the proper math.

items.q: What is the Difference Between GP Sold and GP Received?
items.a: GP Sold is the total expected GP from bookings you've quoted and converted. GP Received is the slice of that GP that's actually arrived as cash from customers. Commission is paid on GP Received only — cash in, cash out. It can be a bit slower than the old way, but it lines up your pay with the company's actual cash flow.

items.q: What if a Client Adds Extra Services or Bumps Up Their Booking? Do I Need to Email About a Catch-Up Commission?
items.a: No more chasing. No more emails. Under the old plan, if a client added an extra performer, extended their booking, or bumped up their package after confirmation, you'd have to flag it so the team could manually adjust your commission. Easy to miss, awkward to ask about. Under the new plan it just sorts itself out: commission is paid on GP Received, so whatever cash actually lands in MEC's account on a booking is what gets attributed to you — including any add-ons, upgrades, or extras the client paid for along the way. They added a saxophonist? Extra cash arrives → extra commission flows to you next cycle, automatically. They cancelled an add-on? Refunded amount nets off, also automatically. Win on both sides — you don't have to email anyone, and the books always tell the truth.

items.q: Why Are My Commissions Inclusive of Super?
items.a: Short answer: when your dashboard shows $1,000 in commission, that $1,000 is the full amount paid in your name. Roughly $890 of it lands in your bank account on payday (pre-tax — the tax man does find that one). The other $110 slips quietly into your super fund — call it the future-you-on-a-beach-with-a-margarita-at-70 fund, and the slice the tax man can't touch on the way in. Both halves are your money; the super part is just locked away until you're 60, the government's quiet way of making sure you don't spend it all on a bender. Why we display it this way: the number on your dashboard is the whole package — what MEC actually pays in your name, full stop. No 'plus 12% super on top', no mental math, no asterisks.

items.q: What About KPIs — When Do They Affect my Pay?
items.a: Right now, nothing. KPIs are locked at 1.0× for Year 1, so they don't move your variable comp at all. From Year 2, KPIs may apply a multiplier somewhere between 0.7× and 1.3× based on your scorecard. The full draft scorecard is on the KPIs tab — read it now, push back, ask questions. We'd rather sort it before activation than after.

items.q: Will my Plan Change Next Year?
items.a: Expect annual band tweaks based on what we've learned and where the business is heading. Bigger structural changes (new shape, team-pool kickers, etc.) get communicated well in advance and are never applied retrospectively. Cash you've already earned is locked in — that's a hard rule, not a soft one.

items.q: What if a Number Looks Wrong or My Pay Seems Off?
items.a: Tell Hayley or Nathan straight away — the sooner the better. Bring the specific figure, what you expected to see, and a Zoho or Xero screenshot if you've got one. We'd much rather find the bug than have you underpaid for a month. Your base salary is never the variable here, so any discrepancy will be in the commission line.

items.q: Where Does the Dashboard Data Come From?
items.a: GP and bookings data flows in from Zoho. Company-level P&L data flows in from Xero. Numbers refresh at the start of each pay cycle. The dashboard is read-only — to change a number on here, the source system has to be updated first. No spreadsheet middleman.

items.q: Who Calculates and Inputs the Actual Data?
items.a: Payroll administration staff grab the actual data from Zoho, which is sent to Hayley for approval — then to Nathan for payment. The dashboard pulls automatically from Zoho (GP, payments) and Xero (P&L), so humans aren't hand-keying numbers — fewer fat-finger mistakes. If a figure looks off, raise it with Hayley or Nathan immediately and we'll trace the source together.

items.q: Is There a Ceiling on the Bonus / Variable Comp?
items.a: No cap. The harder you push, the more you earn per dollar — that's deliberate. Bigger numbers mean higher band rates mean bigger commission cheques. If you want to chase a wild year, the system is built to reward it, not box you in.

items.q: Are Commission Figures Audited?
items.a: Yes — back-audited. As part of each pay cycle the previous months are checked for any errors. But because the new plan is cash-received, any adjustments only ever flow forward — a refund this month reduces a future commission, never claws back from money already in your bank. Annual true-up at year-end catches any drift. Trust, but verify — applies to both sides.

items.q: What Changed About How My GP is Counted? (GP Sold vs GP Received)
items.a: Under the old plan, you got commission the moment a booking was confirmed — based on GP Sold. The new plan ties commission to GP Received: cash that has actually arrived at MEC from the customer. Quotes don't pay. Confirmed bookings don't pay. Cash that lands in MEC's account pays. Yes, this means commission can land later than it used to (especially for events booked far in advance) — but it also means the business pays you out of money it's actually holding, not money it's still waiting for. Healthier for everyone.

items.q: What is GP Attribution and How Does the Payments Module Work?
items.a: When a client pays in instalments — say a deposit now and the balance later — Zoho splits the booking's total expected GP across each payment in proportion to its share of the total. So a $1,000 deposit on a $3,000 booking gives you a third of the GP attributed to that payment, hitting your commission for the month it landed. The remaining two-thirds come through when the balance arrives. The Payments module in Zoho is where you can see exactly how each dollar of GP got attributed back to which payment, and which booking, and which person.

items.q: What About Bookings Confirmed Under the Old Plan? Will I Get Commission Twice?
items.a: No double-dipping in either direction. If your booking was confirmed BEFORE the new plan's effective date and you already received commission under the old 'paid on confirmation' scheme, that's it — you've been paid. The customer's eventual payment doesn't trigger a second commission. So a wedding booked in May 2026 (old plan, paid on confirmation) but happening in October 2026 — the eventual cash arriving in MEC's account doesn't pay you again. On the flip side: GP-attributed commission still flows on bookings CONFIRMED after the effective date, even if the event itself is later in the year. The cutoff is the booking confirmation date, not the event date.

items.q: What if I Leave MEC Mid-quarter?
items.a: Anything already in your bank account stays in your bank account — no clawbacks. Commission earned on cash that's already arrived at MEC but hasn't been paid out yet is yours, and lands in your final paycheck. Cash that arrives at MEC after your last day stays with the company. Base salary is never touched. We try to keep it fair on both sides of the door.

items.q: What Happens to my Commission if my Employment Ends?
items.a: Anything already in your bank account stays in your bank account — no clawbacks. Commission earned on cash that's already arrived at MEC but hasn't been paid out yet is yours, and lands in your final paycheck. Cash that arrives at MEC after your last day stays with the company. Base salary is never touched. We try to keep it fair on both sides of the door.

items.q: What is the Production Gate? Why Does It Exist?
items.a: Your role has both sales and production responsibilities. The production gate sets a minimum annual Event GP Produced target (the GP you have shepherded through to actual event date). The gate ensures we are paying you for both sides of your role — not just Sales-style commission when you have not done the production side.

items.q: What Happens if I Do Not Hit the Production Gate?
items.a: Below the floor ($150k Event GP) no Sales commission is paid (Production Commission of 1% on Event GP still flows). Between floor and full ($300k), Sales commission ramps linearly from 0% up to 100%. At full rate ($300k+), full Sales commission flows. You can see the ramp on your Planning area.

items.q: Why is my Plan Based on Contribution Margin (CM) and Net Profit (NP), Not Personal GP?
items.a: As GM your job is to make the whole business work — not to personally generate sales. Tying your variable comp to business-level metrics aligns your incentives with what is good for the company overall, not just one rep's funnel.

items.q: What is Contribution Margin (CM)?
items.a: Revenue minus all direct costs of doing the work — talent fees, cost of goods sold, anything that scales with the gig. CM is what is left after the work is done, before fixed costs like salaries, rent, software.

items.q: What is Net Profit (NP)?
items.a: CM minus all fixed costs (salaries, rent, software, etc.). NP is what is left for the business after every cost is paid for.

items.q: When Does my CM Band Start Paying?
items.a: Your CM bands kick in at $1.0M of annual CM. Below $1.0M no variable comp flows from CM. From $1.0M-$1.1M you earn 10%. From $1.1M-$1.4M the rate is 5%. Above $1.4M the rate climbs back to 7.5%.

items.q: Why is the Rate Lower in the $1.1M-$1.4M Zone?
items.a: The $1.0M to $1.1M band is where your higher base salary (effective April 2026) is being paid back. The trough at 5% reflects the cost of the uplift — once you have grown CM beyond $1.4M, the rate climbs again to 7.5% to reward the stretch.

items.q: How Does my NP Kicker Work?
items.a: On top of CM commission, an NP-tied kicker scales with annual Net Profit. NP bonuses ramp from $0 to $30k at $1.5M annual NP — see the NP bonus card on your Overview tab for the band structure.

items.q: When Do I Get Paid Commission?
items.a: First fortnightly pay cycle of the quarter — once a quarter, not monthly. Your variable comp is built from quarterly Contribution Margin and Net Profit, so we wait for the full quarter to close before calculating and paying out. The Payments module in Zoho still tracks every dollar back to the source.

items.q: What if a Quarter is Bad?
items.a: Your trailing-12-month CM smooths quarterly variation — one bad quarter does not zero you out, but a sustained drop will reduce variable comp. Your base salary does not move.

items.q: What About KPIs — When Do They Affect my Pay?
items.a: Right now, nothing. KPIs are locked at 1.0× for Year 1, so they don't move your variable comp at all. From Year 2, KPIs may apply a multiplier somewhere between 0.7× and 1.3× based on your scorecard. The full draft scorecard is on the KPIs tab — read it now, push back, ask questions. We'd rather sort it before activation than after.

items.q: What if a Number Looks Wrong or My Pay Seems Off?
items.a: Tell the director (Nathan) straight away — the sooner the better. Bring the specific figure, what you expected to see, and a Zoho or Xero screenshot if you've got one. We'd much rather find the bug than have you underpaid for a month. Your base salary is never the variable here, so any discrepancy will be in the commission line.

items.q: Where Does the Dashboard Data Come From?
items.a: GP and bookings data flows in from Zoho. Company-level P&L data flows in from Xero. Numbers refresh at the start of each pay cycle. The dashboard is read-only — to change a number on here, the source system has to be updated first. No spreadsheet middleman.

items.q: Who Calculates and Inputs the Actual Data?
items.a: Payroll administration staff grab the actual data from Zoho, which is sent to Hayley for approval — then to Nathan for payment. The dashboard pulls automatically from Zoho (GP, payments) and Xero (P&L), so humans aren't hand-keying numbers — fewer fat-finger mistakes. If a figure looks off, raise it with Hayley or Nathan immediately and we'll trace the source together.

items.q: Is There a Ceiling on the Bonus / Variable Comp?
items.a: No cap. The harder you push, the more you earn per dollar — that's deliberate. Bigger numbers mean higher band rates mean bigger commission cheques. If you want to chase a wild year, the system is built to reward it, not box you in.

items.q: Are Commission Figures Audited?
items.a: Yes — back-audited. As part of each pay cycle the previous months are checked for any errors. But because the new plan is cash-received, any adjustments only ever flow forward — a refund this month reduces a future commission, never claws back from money already in your bank. Annual true-up at year-end catches any drift. Trust, but verify — applies to both sides.

items.q: Why Are My Commissions Inclusive of Super?
items.a: Short answer: when your dashboard shows $1,000 in commission, that $1,000 is the full amount paid in your name. Roughly $890 of it lands in your bank account on payday (pre-tax — the tax man does find that one). The other $110 slips quietly into your super fund — call it the future-you-on-a-beach-with-a-margarita-at-70 fund, and the slice the tax man can't touch on the way in. Both halves are your money; the super part is just locked away until you're 60, the government's quiet way of making sure you don't spend it all on a bender. Why we display it this way: the number on your dashboard is the whole package — what MEC actually pays in your name, full stop. No 'plus 12% super on top', no mental math, no asterisks.

items.q: What Changed About How My GP is Counted? (GP Sold vs GP Received)
items.a: Under the old plan, you got commission the moment a booking was confirmed — based on GP Sold. The new plan ties commission to GP Received: cash that has actually arrived at MEC from the customer. Quotes don't pay. Confirmed bookings don't pay. Cash that lands in MEC's account pays. Yes, this means commission can land later than it used to (especially for events booked far in advance) — but it also means the business pays you out of money it's actually holding, not money it's still waiting for. Healthier for everyone.

items.q: What if a Client Adds Extra Services or Bumps Up Their Booking? Do I Need to Email About a Catch-Up Commission?
items.a: No more chasing. No more emails. Under the old plan, if a client added an extra performer, extended their booking, or bumped up their package after confirmation, you'd have to flag it so the team could manually adjust your commission. Easy to miss, awkward to ask about. Under the new plan it just sorts itself out: commission is paid on GP Received, so whatever cash actually lands in MEC's account on a booking is what gets attributed to you — including any add-ons, upgrades, or extras the client paid for along the way. They added a saxophonist? Extra cash arrives → extra commission flows to you next cycle, automatically. They cancelled an add-on? Refunded amount nets off, also automatically. Win on both sides — you don't have to email anyone, and the books always tell the truth.

items.q: What is GP Attribution and How Does the Payments Module Work?
items.a: When a client pays in instalments — say a deposit now and the balance later — Zoho splits the booking's total expected GP across each payment in proportion to its share of the total. So a $1,000 deposit on a $3,000 booking gives you a third of the GP attributed to that payment, hitting your commission for the month it landed. The remaining two-thirds come through when the balance arrives. The Payments module in Zoho is where you can see exactly how each dollar of GP got attributed back to which payment, and which booking, and which person.

items.q: What About Bookings Confirmed Under the Old Plan? Will I Get Commission Twice?
items.a: No double-dipping in either direction. If your booking was confirmed BEFORE the new plan's effective date and you already received commission under the old 'paid on confirmation' scheme, that's it — you've been paid. The customer's eventual payment doesn't trigger a second commission. So a wedding booked in May 2026 (old plan, paid on confirmation) but happening in October 2026 — the eventual cash arriving in MEC's account doesn't pay you again. On the flip side: GP-attributed commission still flows on bookings CONFIRMED after the effective date, even if the event itself is later in the year. The cutoff is the booking confirmation date, not the event date.

items.q: What if I Leave MEC Mid-quarter?
items.a: Different to the sales team: because your variable comp is calculated quarterly (and the quarter hasn't fully landed yet), you need to be employed through the end of the quarter to be eligible for that quarter's commission. If you leave mid-quarter, that quarter's commission doesn't pay out. Anything from previous fully-completed quarters is yours and lands in your final paycheck. Base salary is never touched.

items.q: What Happens to my Commission if my Employment Ends?
items.a: Same logic as the mid-quarter answer above: any commission already paid out to you stays with you — no clawbacks. The current in-progress quarter only pays out if you're employed at the end of it (your plan is calculated on the full quarter's results). Any previous quarter's amounts already calculated but not yet paid land in your final paycheck. Base salary is never touched.

items.q: How is my Commission Different From a Pure Sales Rep?
items.a: Your bands are calculated from Performance Revenue (revenue you bring in as a performer) rather than GP Sold. Performer economics are different — you typically earn more per dollar of revenue than a Sales rep earns per dollar of GP, because the cost structure of a performance is different to a sale.

items.q: What Counts as Performance Revenue?
items.a: Total revenue (ex-GST) from your personally-booked performances over the period. Every gig you perform contributes to your annual Performance Revenue figure.

items.q: What if I Step In for Another Performer Last-Minute?
items.a: You're looked after. Performance Revenue is attributed to whoever actually performed the gig — so if you cover for someone else and you're the one on the floor, the revenue (and the commission) flow to you, not to whoever was originally rostered. The Talent Manager updates the booking in Zoho to reflect who performed; the cash trail follows. No paperwork on your end — just turn up and do your thing.

items.q: When Do I Get Paid Commission?
items.a: First fortnightly pay cycle of the quarter — once a quarter, not monthly. Your performance revenue is reconciled at quarter-end, so we wait for the full quarter to land before calculating and paying out. (Different cycle to the sales team — they're paid monthly.)

items.q: What if a Gig Gets Cancelled or Refunded?
items.a: Refunds aren't fun, but here's how it works: the refunded amount shows as negative cash on the gig in Zoho, and gets netted against your next commission cycle. Your base salary is never touched, and your paycheck never goes negative. (And honestly — have you ever had to process a refund on one of your own gigs? They're extremely rare. We back you to do a great job, and the dashboard math is just here for the edge cases.)

items.q: What About Sales-side Responsibilities?
items.a: If your role includes sales contributions, those are tracked separately on the Planning tab. Sales-side GP feeds into a separate calculation that runs alongside your performance-based commission.

items.q: Will my Plan Change Next Year?
items.a: Expect annual band tweaks based on what we've learned and where the business is heading. Bigger structural changes (new shape, team-pool kickers, etc.) get communicated well in advance and are never applied retrospectively. Cash you've already earned is locked in — that's a hard rule, not a soft one.
